type: viewpoint; also manner — in terms of money
position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint (*Financially, it works*); before an adjective (*financially stable*); end after a verb (*support them financially*)
modifies: whole clauses, adjectives and participles, verbs
form: -ly from *financial*; the first syllable is also said *fy-*
contrast: Russian *материально помогать* is *help financially*, not *materially* — English *materially* means significantly (*it did not materially change the result*).

senses.gloss: From the point of view of money; when money is considered.
senses.ru: с финансовой точки зрения, в финансовом плане
examples: *Financially*, the move to Texas made a lot of sense.
The plan looks good *financially*, but it will take years.
*Financially*, we're in much better shape than last year.

senses.gloss: In a way that concerns money — having it, earning it, or giving it.
examples: My parents still support me *financially*.
She wants to be *financially* independent by thirty.
A lot of families are struggling *financially* right now.

type: viewpoint; also manner — in terms of politics
position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint; before an adjective or participle (*politically active*)
modifies: whole clauses, adjectives and participles, verbs
form: -ly from *political*; the *-al-* is usually not pronounced: *puh-LIT-ik-lee*
contrast: *Politically correct* is a fixed phrase: avoiding words that could offend a group, often said with irony. It does not mean correct from a political point of view. Its opposite is *politically incorrect*.

senses.gloss: From a political point of view; when politics or public opinion is considered.
examples: *Politically*, raising taxes right before an election would be suicide.
The plan makes sense on paper, but *politically* it's a nonstarter.
*Politically*, the governor can't afford to lose the suburbs.

senses.gloss: In a way connected with politics, government, or political parties.
examples: My grandmother was *politically* active her whole life.
Police say the attack was *politically* motivated.
It's one of the most *politically* divided states in the country.

position: any position — front with a comma for 'strictly speaking' (*Technically, …*); mid (*it's technically legal*); before an adjective (*technically difficult*)
form: -ly from *technical*; the *-al-* is usually not pronounced: *TEK-nik-lee*
contrast: The most common American sense has nothing to do with technology: *Technically, he's still my boss* means формально — the rules say so, though real life may differ, and a *but* often follows. Russian *технически* covers only sense 2. Don't confuse it with *practically* or *virtually*, which mean almost.

senses.gloss: According to the exact rules or the strict meaning of words, even if not in reality.
examples: *Technically*, you're still married until the judge signs the papers.
It's *technically* legal, but it's a terrible idea.
*Technically*, the store closes at nine, but they let people finish shopping.

senses.gloss: In terms of technology or technique — the equipment and methods involved, or the skill shown in an art, sport, or craft.
senses.ru: технически, с технической точки зрения, в плане техники
examples: *Technically*, the new phone is a big step forward.
The bridge was *technically* difficult to build.
She's a *technically* brilliant pianist, but her playing feels cold.

position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint; before an adjective (*legally binding*); end after a verb (*buy it legally*)
modifies: whole clauses, adjectives and participles, verbs
form: -ly from *legal*
contrast: *Legally blind* is an American legal category — sight so poor (20/200 or worse with glasses) that a person qualifies for benefits — not total blindness. Where Russian says *юридически*, English says *legally*: *legally binding* is юридически обязывающий.

senses.gloss: From the point of view of the law; as far as the law is concerned.
examples: *Legally*, the landlord has to return your deposit within 30 days.
Once you sign it, the contract is *legally* binding.
Parents are *legally* responsible for getting their kids to school.

senses.gloss: In a way that is allowed by law.
examples: You can't *legally* park here after 6 p.m.
You have to be 21 to buy alcohol *legally*.
He came into the country *legally*.

position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint; before an adjective or participle (*medically necessary*); end after a verb (*treated medically*)
modifies: whole clauses, adjectives and participles, verbs
form: -ly from *medical*; the *-al-* is usually not pronounced: *MED-ik-lee*
contrast: *Medically* is about medicine as a field; *medicinally* means as a medicine (*herbs used medicinally*). In American health insurance, *medically necessary* is a fixed term for the care a plan has to pay for.

senses.gloss: From a medical point of view; in terms of health and medicine.
examples: *Medically*, there's nothing wrong with him — the pain may be stress.
Insurance only covers the surgery if it's *medically* necessary.
She was *medically* cleared to play on Saturday.

senses.gloss: By means of medical treatment, especially drugs rather than surgery.
examples: Most cases can be managed *medically* without an operation.
The patient was put in a *medically* induced coma.

position: any position — front with a comma for an opinion (*Personally, I…*); mid before the verb for 'yourself' (*she personally called*); end after *take it* or *know someone*
comparison: not gradable — except *take it very personally*
form: -ly from *personal*; double *l*
contrast: *Personally* is not *in person*: *I met him in person* means face to face; *I know him personally* means we are acquainted, not just by name. *Take it personally* is the set phrase for принимать на свой счёт. The opinion sense almost always goes with *I* or *we*: *Personally, I think…*.

senses.gloss: Used to show that you are giving your own opinion.
examples: *Personally*, I think the first movie was better.
I don't care for sushi *personally*, but the kids love it.
*Personally*, I'd wait until the price drops.

senses.gloss: By yourself, not through someone else.
examples: The mayor *personally* called to apologize.
I'll deliver the check *personally*.
You'll be *personally* responsible for the equipment.

senses.gloss: As a person — in terms of character or a private relationship, not a professional or public role.
examples: I don't know the senator *personally*, only from the news.
The two candidates dislike each other *personally*, not just politically.

senses.gloss: As an attack on or criticism of yourself, especially in *take something personally*.
examples: Don't take it *personally* — he's rude to everyone.
She took the rejection very *personally*.

position: any position — front with a comma; mid (*you could theoretically*); before an adjective (*it's theoretically possible*)
form: -ly from *theoretical*; the *-al-* is usually not pronounced
contrast: Like *technically*, sense 1 hints that reality is different: *Theoretically, it's possible* usually means don't count on it. The natural partner is *in practice*: *Theoretically…, but in practice…*.

senses.gloss: In theory — according to what should happen, though it may not happen in practice.
examples: *Theoretically*, the drive takes three hours, but not with Friday traffic.
It's *theoretically* possible to see the northern lights from Chicago.
*Theoretically*, anyone can apply for the job.

senses.gloss: In terms of theory; from the standpoint of an academic or scientific theory.
examples: The paper is *theoretically* interesting but has very little data.
Her research is *theoretically* grounded in behavioral economics.

position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint; before an adjective (*statistically significant*)
form: -ly from *statistical*; the *-al-* is usually not pronounced
contrast: *Statistically significant* is a technical term — unlikely to be the result of chance. It is not a synonym of large or important: a tiny difference can be statistically significant.

senses.gloss: According to statistics; when you look at the numbers.
examples: *Statistically*, flying is much safer than driving.
*Statistically*, most new restaurants close within a few years.
Young men are *statistically* more likely to get into car accidents.

senses.gloss: By the methods of statistics.
examples: The difference between the two groups was not *statistically* significant.
The survey results were analyzed *statistically*.

position: any position — front with a comma for 'in the past'; mid (*have historically outperformed*); before an adjective (*historically accurate*)
form: -ly from both *historic* and *historical*; the *-al-* is usually not pronounced
contrast: One adverb serves two adjectives: *historic* (important in history) and *historical* (about history), so both *historically important* and *historically accurate*. In sense 1 the tense shows whether the pattern goes on: present perfect if it still does (*Historically, the state has voted Democratic*), past simple if it has ended (*Historically, women were paid less*). In American English the article is *a*, not *an*: *a historically important building*.

senses.gloss: In the past, over a long period; traditionally; also compared with the past (*historically low*).
examples: *Historically*, this neighborhood has been home to Italian immigrants.
Mortgage rates hit *historically* low levels during the pandemic.
*Historically*, women were paid less for the same work.

senses.gloss: In terms of history; from the point of view of a historian.
examples: The movie isn't very *historically* accurate.
It's a *historically* important building — the treaty was signed here.
*Historically*, the Battle of Gettysburg was the turning point of the Civil War.

position: any position — front with a comma; before an adjective (*culturally diverse*)
form: -ly from *cultural*; double *l*
contrast: False friend: Russian *культурно* (вести себя культурно) means politely, with good manners — English *politely*, *decently*. *Culturally* only means in terms of culture.

senses.gloss: In terms of a society's customs, traditions, and beliefs.
senses.ru: в культурном отношении, с точки зрения культуры
examples: *Culturally*, the two countries have a lot in common.
Our school is *culturally* diverse — the kids speak twenty languages at home.
In some places it isn't *culturally* acceptable to refuse food from a host.

senses.gloss: In terms of the arts — music, theater, museums, and literature.
examples: *Culturally*, Chicago has as much to offer as New York.
The town is small but *culturally* rich, with two theaters and a jazz club.

position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint; before an adjective (*economically viable*); end after a verb for 'thriftily' (*live economically*)
comparison: more/most — only in the 'thriftily' sense (*more economically*); not gradable as a viewpoint
modifies: whole clauses, adjectives and participles, verbs
form: -ly from both *economic* (about the economy) and *economical* (saving money); also said *ee-kuh-NAHM-ik-lee*
contrast: The two senses belong to two adjectives: *economic growth* (экономический) but *an economical car* (экономичный). The adverb is the same word, so context decides: *economically weak* is экономически слабый; *use it economically* is экономно.

senses.gloss: In terms of the economy, trade, or wealth.
examples: *Economically*, the town never recovered after the plant closed.
The project isn't *economically* viable without federal money.
Kids from *economically* disadvantaged families get free lunch.

senses.gloss: In a way that uses little money, time, or material, without waste.
examples: We're trying to live more *economically* until I find a new job.
Use the paint *economically* — it's all we have.
She writes *economically*, never wasting a word.

position: any position — front with a comma; before an adjective (*logistically difficult*)
form: -ly from *logistical*; the first syllable is also said *loh-*
contrast: Not related to logic: *logically* is логично, по логике; *logistically* is about planning, transport, and supplies. *Logistically impossible* means it can't be organized, not that it makes no sense.

senses.gloss: In terms of the practical planning and organization of people, transport, and supplies.
senses.ru: с организационной точки зрения, в плане логистики
examples: *Logistically*, getting 200 guests to an island is a nightmare.
The move was *logistically* complicated, with three trucks and two dogs.
It's a great idea, but *logistically* we can't pull it off by June.

position: any position — front with a comma; before an adjective (*structurally sound*); end after a verb (*changed structurally*)
form: -ly from *structural*; double *l*
contrast: In engineering Russian, *конструктивно* (по конструкции) is *structurally* or *in design* — not *constructively*, which in English only means in a helpful way (*constructive criticism*). *Structurally sound* is the set phrase for a building that is safe and not about to fall down.

senses.gloss: In terms of how a building, bridge, or object is built and holds together.
examples: The inspector said the house is *structurally* sound.
The bridge was *structurally* damaged in the earthquake.
*Structurally*, the old barn is in better shape than it looks.

senses.gloss: In terms of the way the parts of a system, text, or organization are arranged.
examples: *Structurally*, the novel moves between three timelines.
English and German are *structurally* similar.
The economy has changed *structurally* since the 1980s.

position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint; before an adjective or participle (*scientifically proven*); end after a verb (*test it scientifically*)
comparison: more/most — in the 'by scientific methods' sense (*more scientifically*); not gradable as a viewpoint
modifies: whole clauses, adjectives and participles, verbs
form: -ally from *scientific* (there is no *scientifical*); the ending is said *-ik-lee*

senses.gloss: According to science; from a scientific point of view.
examples: *Scientifically*, there's no evidence that the diet works.
It's *scientifically* proven that smoking causes cancer.
The ad's claims aren't *scientifically* accurate.

senses.gloss: Using the careful, systematic methods of science.
examples: The drug has never been *scientifically* tested on children.
We need to approach the problem more *scientifically*, one variable at a time.

position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint; before an adjective (*morally wrong*); end after a verb (*act morally*)
comparison: more/most — in the 'rightly' sense (*more morally*); not gradable as a viewpoint
form: -ly from *moral*; double *l*
contrast: False friend: Russian *морально* often means emotionally or mentally — *морально тяжело* is *emotionally draining*, *морально подготовиться* is *prepare mentally*, *морально устал* is *mentally exhausted*, and *морально устаревший* is *outdated* or *obsolete*. English *morally* is only about right and wrong; *moral support* is the one place the two languages match.

senses.gloss: From the point of view of right and wrong.
examples: *Morally*, what he did was wrong, even if it was legal.
I think it's *morally* unacceptable to lie to a patient.
Is the company *morally* responsible for the spill?

senses.gloss: In a way that is right and good; by high moral standards.
examples: She tried to live *morally* in a business full of cheats.
Most people believe they behave more *morally* than their neighbors.

position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint; before an adjective (*socially acceptable*); end after a verb (*see someone socially*)
form: -ly from *social*; double *l*
contrast: *I drink socially* means only at parties and dinners with friends, not alone and not much — it has nothing to do with drinking in public. Don't confuse *socially* with *sociably* (in a friendly, outgoing way).

senses.gloss: In terms of society, social class, or what people in general accept.
examples: Smoking indoors is no longer *socially* acceptable.
*Socially*, smartphones have changed how teenagers date.
The program helps *socially* disadvantaged kids get into college.

senses.gloss: In situations where people meet for pleasure, outside work or duty.
senses.ru: в компании, в неформальной обстановке, вне работы
examples: We work together, but we never see each other *socially*.
I only drink *socially*, maybe a beer at a barbecue.
It's hard to meet people *socially* after you move to a new city.

senses.gloss: In terms of relationships with other people and the ability to get along with them.
examples: He's brilliant but *socially* awkward.
Our daughter did fine academically but struggled *socially* in middle school.

position: any position — before an adjective (*emotionally exhausted*); front with a comma as a viewpoint; end after a verb (*speak emotionally*)
comparison: more/most — in the 'with strong feeling' sense (*more emotionally*); not gradable as a viewpoint
modifies: adjectives and participles, whole clauses, verbs
form: -ly from *emotional*; double *l*
contrast: This is where Russian *морально* usually belongs: *морально тяжело* is *emotionally hard* or *draining*, *моральная травма* is *emotional trauma*. Translating it as *morally* turns it into a question of right and wrong.

senses.gloss: In terms of feelings; with regard to a person's emotional state.
examples: After the funeral I was *emotionally* exhausted.
*Emotionally*, she's still not ready to date again.
Caring for a sick parent is *emotionally* draining.

senses.gloss: In a way that shows strong feelings.
examples: He spoke *emotionally* about his late father.
Fans reacted *emotionally* when the team finally won the title.

position: any position — before an adjective (*physically fit*); front with a comma as a viewpoint; mid before a verb (*physically attacked*)
modifies: adjectives and participles, whole clauses, verbs
form: -ly from *physical*; the *-al-* is usually not pronounced: *FIZ-ik-lee*
contrast: In everyday English *physically* is about the body or the material world; for the school subject say *in terms of physics*. In casual American speech *I physically can't* is an exaggeration for I really can't.

senses.gloss: In terms of the body rather than the mind.
examples: You need to be *physically* fit to join the fire department.
*Physically*, he's fine — it's his mental health we're worried about.
Construction work is *physically* demanding.

senses.gloss: In terms of material things or actual presence, as opposed to online, on paper, or in the mind.
examples: The company is registered in Delaware but *physically* located in Denver.
Students must be *physically* present to take the exam.

senses.gloss: According to the laws of nature; in reality at all.
examples: It's *physically* impossible to be in two places at once.
There's no way — I *physically* can't finish this by Friday.

position: any position — before an adjective (*mentally ill*); front with a comma as a viewpoint; mid before a verb for 'in your head' (*mentally calculated*)
modifies: adjectives and participles, whole clauses, verbs
form: -ly from *mental*; double *l*
contrast: Russian *морально готов* and *морально устал* are *mentally ready* and *mentally exhausted*, not *morally*. Avoid *mentally retarded*: it is now offensive; American English says *intellectual disability*.

senses.gloss: In terms of the mind or mental health.
examples: Marathon runners have to be *mentally* tough.
He was *mentally* ill for years before anyone noticed.
*Mentally*, I'm ready for the exam; I just need some sleep.

senses.gloss: In your mind, without speaking, writing, or doing anything.
examples: I *mentally* added up the bill while the waiter talked.
She *mentally* went over her speech one more time.

position: any position — mid before the verb (*officially opens*); front with a comma for the public version (*Officially, …*)
modifies: verbs, whole clauses, adjectives and participles
form: -ly from *official*; double *l*
contrast: Russian *официально* also means formal in style — *официально одет* is *formally dressed*, *официальный тон* is *a formal tone*. English *officially* only means by authority or for the record. Sense 3 (*It's officially summer*) is informal but very common in American speech.

senses.gloss: By people in authority or according to the rules; for the record.
examples: The new bridge *officially* opens on Monday.
The White House has not *officially* confirmed the report.
You aren't *officially* enrolled until you pay the fee.

senses.gloss: According to what is said publicly, which may not be the whole truth.
examples: *Officially*, he resigned; everyone knows he was fired.
*Officially*, the trip was about trade, but the senator spent most of it on the beach.

senses.gloss: Informal: now definitely, beyond any doubt.
examples: It's ninety degrees — summer is *officially* here.
I'm *officially* addicted to this show.

position: any position — front with a comma for 'in an ideal world' (*Ideally, …*); mid (*you should ideally*); before a participle for 'perfectly' (*ideally located*)
form: -ly from *ideal*; double *l*
contrast: Russian *идеально* is usually *perfectly*: *идеально убрано* is *perfectly clean*, *всё прошло идеально* is *everything went perfectly*. English *ideally* in that sense goes only with a few participles — *suited*, *located*, *placed*, *positioned*, *situated*. Otherwise *ideally* means in an ideal world.

senses.gloss: In the best possible situation; if things were exactly as you want them.
examples: *Ideally*, we'd leave by six to beat the traffic.
*Ideally*, the new hire would speak Spanish.
You should *ideally* get seven to eight hours of sleep.

senses.gloss: Perfectly; in the best possible way, used with a few participles.
examples: The hotel is *ideally* located, two blocks from the beach.
With all that patience, she's *ideally* suited to teaching.

position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint; before an adjective or participle (*ethically sourced*); end after a verb (*act ethically*)
comparison: more/most — in the 'fairly and honestly' sense (*more ethically*); not gradable as a viewpoint
modifies: whole clauses, adjectives and participles, verbs
form: -ly from *ethical*; the *-al-* is usually not pronounced: *ETH-ik-lee*
contrast: Russian splits *этически* (from the point of view of ethics) and *этично* (in an ethical way); English uses *ethically* for both. *Ethically* is the usual word for professional rules — medicine, law, business, journalism — where *morally* would sound personal or religious.

senses.gloss: From the point of view of moral rules, especially the rules of a profession.
examples: *Ethically*, a therapist can't date a patient.
Paying people for five-star reviews is *ethically* questionable.
The study raises *ethically* difficult questions about privacy.

senses.gloss: In a morally correct and fair way.
examples: We only buy *ethically* sourced coffee.
Companies are under pressure to behave more *ethically*.

position: any position — front with a comma; before an adjective (*geographically close*)
form: -ly from *geographical* or *geographic*; the *-al-* is usually not pronounced

senses.gloss: In terms of location, distance, or the physical features of an area.
examples: *Geographically*, Alaska is closer to Russia than to the rest of the United States.
The two towns are *geographically* close but very different culturally.
Our sales team is *geographically* spread out across four time zones.

position: any position — front with a comma; before an adjective (*biologically related*)
form: -ly from *biological*; the *-al-* is usually not pronounced
contrast: Russian *био-* on food labels (биопродукты) is *organic* in English, not *biologically grown*. Sense 2 is the everyday American use in family talk: *biologically related*, as opposed to adopted or step-.

senses.gloss: In terms of biology; from the point of view of how living things work.
examples: *Biologically*, whales are mammals, not fish.
Teenagers are *biologically* wired to stay up late.
Some of these chemicals stay *biologically* active for years.

senses.gloss: By birth; in terms of genes rather than adoption or marriage.
examples: We're not *biologically* related — my dad married her mom.
He raised the boy, though he wasn't *biologically* his father.

position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint; before an adjective or participle (*commercially available*); end after a verb (*failed commercially*)
modifies: whole clauses, adjectives and participles, verbs
form: -ly from *commercial*; double *l*
contrast: *Commercially available* means anyone can buy it in stores or online — not that it is expensive, advertised, or sold by a private company. Russian *коммерческий* in the sense of paid or private (*коммерческий вуз*) is *private* or *for-profit*, not *commercial*.

senses.gloss: In terms of making money; as a business.
examples: The film was loved by critics but failed *commercially*.
*Commercially*, it was the band's biggest album.
It's a great invention, but is it *commercially* viable?

senses.gloss: Made, grown, or offered for sale to the public, rather than privately or for research.
examples: The vaccine won't be *commercially* available until next year.
Most *commercially* grown tomatoes are picked before they're ripe.

position: any position — before an adjective (*environmentally friendly*); front with a comma
form: -ly from *environmental*; double *l*
contrast: Russian *экологически чистый* is *environmentally friendly* for a product and *clean* or *organic* for food or a place; *плохая экология* is *pollution*, not *bad ecology*. In everyday American English *environmentally* is far more common than *ecologically*, which sounds scientific.

senses.gloss: In terms of the natural world and its protection.
examples: Paper straws are more *environmentally* friendly than plastic ones.
*Environmentally*, the new pipeline is a disaster waiting to happen.
The wetlands are *environmentally* sensitive, so building there is restricted.

senses.gloss: Caused by surroundings and living conditions rather than by genes.
examples: Doctors don't know whether the disease is inherited or *environmentally* caused.
Some asthma attacks are *environmentally* triggered.

position: any position — front with a comma as a viewpoint; before an adjective (*visually stunning*); end after a verb (*inspected visually*)
modifies: whole clauses, adjectives and participles, verbs
form: -ly from *visual*; double *l*
contrast: Russian *визуально* is often everyday speech for by the look of it — *визуально всё в порядке* is *it looks fine*, and *знать визуально* is *know by sight*. English *visually* is more formal and technical. *Visually impaired* is the polite American term for people who are blind or partly blind.

senses.gloss: In terms of how something looks.
examples: *Visually*, the movie is stunning, but the story is thin.
The new website is much more *visually* appealing.
The two apps are *visually* almost identical.

senses.gloss: By looking, or in terms of the ability to see.
examples: The mechanic checked the brakes *visually* before the test drive.
The software helps *visually* impaired students read their textbooks.
